items.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006
items.q: The interviewee discusses John Coltrane's musical analysis and influences extensively but does not claim a personal relationship, stating 'I know for a fact that that was something that he discovered' and recounting stories told by others or general knowledge.

ctx.x: Do you somehow try to find a scale or a sound that’s both?

Yeah. And that gets back to, again, my analysis. You know like when you’re analyzing harmony or the melody, see those things fit together. I mean in other words if you’re just thinking about it okay, going down in half-steps you know, you’ll miss it. Dominant sevenths by their very nature, I don’t know if I’m getting too analytical. They’re really interesting when you think about them because they have different qualities about them in a dominant seventh, especially when John Coltrane was dealing with them. They…

is the major chord and then G-B-flat, you know, E-G-B-flat which is the half diminished. And then if you start extending them then you know they have minor qualities about them, you know like say for instance I remember when I was analyzing “Blue Trane” and there was one passage on like a C7 type of chord where John played a minor eleventh. And so he played like B-flat, D-flat, F, A-flat, E-flat, G, right? And so I’m analyzing and I say well wow, well B-flat is the seventh, the D-flat could either be you know the…
